summary: Can the array be split into two subsets with equal sums?
mainInsight: If the total is odd the answer is False. Otherwise it is the subset-sum problem with target total / 2: dp[s] is true if some subset sums to s. Iterate numbers and sums downwards so each number is used once: for s from target down to x, dp[s] |= dp[s - x].
commonMistakes: Using the full sum as the target

promptVariants: Why does the problem reduce to a subset-sum with target sum / 2?
options: One subset summing to total / 2 leaves the other the same; odd totals fail
The two subsets must have equal sizes, so choose n / 2 items
The largest element must be at most half of the total
Every element of the array must be even to split it
cards.answer: One subset summing to total / 2 leaves the other the same; odd totals fail

incorrectOptionExplanations.The two subsets must have equal sizes, s: Only the sums must be equal.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Every element of the array must be even: Odd numbers can still pair up.

promptVariants: Why must the 1D DP iterate sums downwards?
What goes wrong when iterating upwards?
cards.answer: Updating dp[s] from dp[s - x] in increasing order lets the same number x be used several times in one pass (dp[s - x] has already been updated with x), turning it into an unbounded knapsack. Iterating downwards reads only values from the previous item, so each number is used once.
cards.explanation: A Python int bitset (dp |= dp << x) is a neat alternative.
For each number update up to S/2 sums.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Space complexity (excluding the input): ___
cards.explanation: A boolean array of size sum / 2 + 1.

promptVariants: What does the algorithm return for [1, 5, 11, 5]?
options: False: the array contains a very large element
True: [1, 5] and [11, 5] both sum to 6 and 16
